title: DVLA — the patient who won't stop driving

scenario.applicant_role: You are not in this scenario. You are being asked to reason about a situation a doctor faces. You are not expected to know the law.
scenario.opening_prompt: A doctor has told a patient that a recent diagnosis means they must inform the DVLA and stop driving. At the next appointment the patient says they have not told the DVLA and are still driving to work. What should the doctor be thinking about?
scenario.candidate_brief: You have one minute to read this before the station begins.

expected_content.point: Recognises the legal duty to notify sits with the DRIVER, not the doctor
evidence_cues: it's their responsibility to tell the DVLA

expected_content.point: The doctor's first move is to explain the duty and make every reasonable effort to persuade the patient to stop
Identifies WHY the patient might be refusing — work, independence, caring responsibilities — rather than treating refusal as obstinacy
evidence_cues: they might need it for work
what's driving losing their licence mean for them

expected_content.point: Applies a risk threshold: does continued driving expose OTHERS to a risk of death or serious harm
Treats disclosure as a balance, not an automatic consequence of refusal
Tells the patient before disclosing, where practicable, and confirms in writing afterwards
evidence_cues: tell them I was going to

expected_content.point: Names confidentiality as the default that is being departed from, and why that default exists
evidence_cues: people need to be able to tell their doctor

optional_strong_points: Distinguishes this public-interest discretion from a statutory duty such as notifiable disease reporting, where no balancing is required
Notes that the doctor should document the decision either way
Recognises the doctor may seek advice from a defence body or a senior colleague first

red_flags.flag: States that the doctor must report the patient to the DVLA, as a legal duty on the doctor
detection_cues: the doctor has to report them
it's the doctor's legal duty to inform

red_flags.flag: Would disclose immediately with no attempt to persuade and no risk assessment
Would take no action at all because confidentiality is absolute
Offers a clinical judgement about whether the condition actually affects driving

model_answer_principles: The sequence matters more than the conclusion: explain, persuade, assess risk to others, warn, disclose, confirm in writing.
Confidentiality is departed from on a balance, not overridden by a rule.
Understanding the refusal is part of managing it, not a preliminary courtesy.

band_descriptors.poor: Jumps straight to reporting, or refuses to consider disclosure at all. No risk reasoning.
band_descriptors.borderline: Reaches the right end point but skips persuasion or the risk-to-others test. May assert the doctor has a legal duty to report.
band_descriptors.competent: Works through the sequence, names risk to others as the threshold, treats disclosure as a balance.
band_descriptors.excellent: All of the above plus the patient's perspective explored, the doctor's onward communication addressed, and confidentiality's purpose articulated rather than named.

planned_followups.prompt: What would you want to know about why they're still driving?
Does it make a difference if they drive a school minibus rather than commuting alone?

conditional_followups.prompt: You've said the doctor might have to break confidentiality. What would have to be true for that to be justified?
Is there any circumstance in which a doctor could share information without consent?
Which two of those are actually pulling against each other here, and what would make one give way?
Suppose the doctor tells the DVLA and it turns out the patient had already notified them. Was the doctor wrong to act?

do_not_lead: risk of death or serious harm
the driver has the legal duty

source_basis.reference: GMC — Patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA, paras 3, 4, 6, 9, 10
source_basis.quote: The driver is legally responsible for telling the DVLA or DVA about any such condition or treatment.

source_basis.reference: GMC Confidentiality, paras 63-68 (public interest) and para 87 (required by law)

wellbeing_rules: Do not ask the candidate about their own or a family member's driving or health

title: The relative who has been waiting (roleplay)

scenario.applicant_role: You are a hospital volunteer on the day-surgery reception desk. You have no access to clinical information, no access to the patient list, and no authority over theatre scheduling. You may speak to the nurse in charge.
scenario.opening_prompt: Marcus Adeyemi is at the desk. His mother came in at seven this morning for day surgery. It is now half past two and he has had no update. Please speak to him.
scenario.candidate_brief: You have one minute to read this. The station lasts seven minutes.

expected_content.point: States their role accurately and early — volunteer, no access to clinical information
Acknowledges the length of the wait and its effect before offering any explanation
evidence_cues: that's a long time with no news

expected_content.point: Asks what he has already been told
Offers a specific, deliverable action — find the nurse in charge, ask for an estimate, take a number
evidence_cues: let me ask the nurse in charge

expected_content.point: Notices and addresses the belief that no news means something has gone wrong, without making any clinical claim
evidence_cues: a long wait doesn't necessarily mean
I can't tell you why, but

expected_content.point: Establishes his own constraints — that he has somewhere to be
evidence_cues: do you need to be somewhere

optional_strong_points: Closes with a named next step and a name
Checks whether he has eaten or needs anything, without being obsequious
Does not over-apologise for something outside their control

red_flags.flag: Speculates about the mother's clinical condition or the reason for the delay
Promises a time or an outcome outside their control
Claims or fails to correct a clinical role
detection_cues: as a member of the team I can tell you
does not correct 'are you a nurse'

red_flags.flag: Tells him to calm down or to sit down before he has been heard
detection_cues: if you could just take a seat

model_answer_principles: Acknowledgement precedes explanation. Explanation before acknowledgement escalates.
'I'm a volunteer' is honest information, not an exit from the conversation.
A small deliverable action outperforms a large sympathetic statement.

trigger.detail: no acknowledgement of the wait in the first 60 seconds

conditional_followups.prompt: [in role] You haven't actually said anything about the fact we've been here since seven.
[in role] So you think something HAS gone wrong?

do_not_lead: the mother's instruction not to make a fuss

hidden_information.fact: He took unpaid leave and must collect his daughter at 3:15.
hidden_information.disclosure_condition: An open question about his situation or time pressure, not about the list.

hidden_information.fact: His mother told him not to make a fuss, which is part of the anger.
hidden_information.disclosure_condition: Only after the anger has already de-escalated.

university_compatibility.excluded_reason: Roleplay confirmed on the institution's own pages only at these schools; served universally in general practice mode but surfaced in university-specific modes only here.

source_basis.reference: QUB MMI candidate information — four of nine assessed stations involve role players
Birmingham — 'Interaction in Healthcare Setting' station with professional role-players
MSC interviews page — MMIs include 'practical scenarios that involve candidates interacting with an actor'

wellbeing_rules: Do not ask the candidate about a relative's surgery or hospital experience

scenario.applicant_role: You are being asked for your reasoning about a contested public question. You are not expected to have a settled view, and you will not be marked on which side you take.
scenario.opening_prompt: Doctors in England have taken industrial action over pay in recent years. Is it ever right for doctors to strike?

expected_content.point: States the case FOR industrial action at its strongest — real-terms pay erosion, retention, and the argument that a sustainable workforce is itself a patient-safety issue
evidence_cues: pay has fallen in real terms

expected_content.point: States the case AGAINST at its strongest — direct harm to patients during action, and the asymmetry that patients did not cause the dispute
Recognises that the profession itself is divided, rather than presenting one view as the medical view
Names a mechanism that mitigates the tension — derogations, emergency cover, notice periods
Gets the current position broadly right, or is appropriately tentative about it
evidence_cues: I think the resident doctors' dispute has been resolved
I'm not sure of the current position but

expected_content.point: Distinguishes the right to withdraw labour from the question of whether exercising it is wise in a given case

optional_strong_points: Notes that consultants and resident doctors are in different positions
Observes that 'patient harm during action' and 'patient harm from an understaffed service' are the same currency and can be compared
Says explicitly what would change their view

red_flags.flag: Refuses to engage on the grounds that the topic is political
Argues only one side and does not engage the opposing case when directly invited to
Disparages doctors who took a different position

model_answer_principles: There is no correct side. The assessment is whether both cases are stated at their strongest and whether the candidate can say what would change their mind.
Accuracy about the current position is expected; precision about figures is not.
Declining to engage is a weak answer, not a neutral one.

band_descriptors.poor: One side only, or refuses to engage. May misstate the current position confidently.
band_descriptors.borderline: Both sides named but one is a strawman. Current position vague or wrong.
band_descriptors.competent: Both cases stated fairly, current position broadly right or appropriately hedged, some mechanism named.
band_descriptors.excellent: As competent, plus the profession's own division acknowledged, a mitigating mechanism engaged with, and an explicit statement of what would change their view.

conditional_followups.prompt: A patient whose cancer surgery was cancelled during a strike would say they had no part in this dispute. What would you say to them?
If pay erosion drives people out of the profession over ten years, is that not also patient harm? How would you weigh the two?

trigger.detail: discussed NHS funding generally without addressing striking

conditional_followups.prompt: That's the context — but is the act of striking itself defensible?
You've held both sides well. Push yourself: what would have to be true for you to change your position?

do_not_lead: any figure the candidate has not raised

university_compatibility.excluded_reason: Served in university-specific mode only where the school publishes current affairs or contemporary awareness as an assessed area.

source_basis.reference: Manchester — 'contemporary medical knowledge' is a published assessed criterion
Sheffield — 'Medicine in a wider context' is a named MMI section; candidates advised to follow 'NHS politics'
BMA — resident doctors in England vote to accept pay and jobs offer, 29 June 2026
NHS Employers — consultants and SAS doctor ballot outcome, 6 July 2026

wellbeing_rules: The interviewer must never signal a position on this topic
Challenge must be applied symmetrically regardless of which side the candidate takes
